name: Addis Foto Fest
overview: Biennial international photography festival in Addis Ababa, with exhibitions, portfolio reviews, conferences, projections and film screenings over about a week.
Founded in 2010 by Aida Muluneh, who directs it. Produced by Desta for Africa Creative Consulting (The Reporter, 2018; the festival's site). Held every other December since 2010 (Wikipedia).
The fifth edition was set to start on 6 December 2018, run five days and bring a record 152 participants from 61 countries (The Reporter, 24 November 2018).
funding_verdict: Addis Foto Fest: privately run as a business; the last sponsor list found (2018) names an embassy and corporate sponsors

name: Villa Skeppet
overview: House museum at Snäcksundsvägen 8 in Ekenäs (Tammisaari), Raseborg, close to the town centre and the Hagen-Ramsholmen nature park. The pages read give no distance.

Alvar Aalto began planning it in spring 1969 for his friends Christine and Göran Schildt and it was built in 1969 to 1970. Wikipedia calls it the last and smallest home he designed. Christine Schildt moved out in 2017, the Christine and Göran Schildt Foundation owns it, and it opened to the public in December 2020.

It was first called Villa Schildt and soon renamed Skeppet ("boat" or "vessel"). A 1971 Västra Nyland quote on the villa's background page describes a ship's prow that rises towards the south bay in Ekenäs.
funding_verdict: Villa Skeppet: foundation-owned: no income, donor or grant list published

press_items.title: Sanna Tegel, "Villa Skeppet, a Building and a Home" (2019)

name: Gallen-Kallela Museum
overview: Artist's studio house and museum at Gallen-Kallelan tie 27 in Tarvaspää, Espoo. The pages read give no distance to Helsinki.

The Akseli Gallen-Kallela Museum Foundation, registered in 1958 by Kirsti, Pirkko and Aivi Gallen-Kallela with the Kalevala Society Foundation and the Finnish Cultural Foundation Support Association, acquired the studio and Villa Linudd in 1958. The museum opened in 1961.
Named for the painter Akseli Gallen-Kallela (1865 to 1931), who designed and built the studio.
funding_verdict: Gallen-Kallela Museum: public and earned money: state museum subsidy, Espoo grants, tickets and sales

name: Didrichsen Art Museum
overview: Art museum and sculpture park beside the founders' home at Kuusilahdenkuja 1 on Kuusisaari island, western Helsinki, by the sea.
Marie-Louise and Gunnar Didrichsen set up the Didrichsen Art Foundation on 11 November 1963, gave it part of their collection, the estate and the building, and opened the museum in 1965.
Named for the founders. Gunnar, born in Copenhagen in 1903, founded the importer Transmeri Ltd.
funding_verdict: Didrichsen Art Museum: foundation-run: tickets, state subsidy and unnamed grants

name: Muuratsalo Experimental House
overview: Studio house and smoke sauna on the western shore of Muuratsalo island in Lake Päijänne, at Melalammentie 2. The island is part of Jyväskylä, and the house is about 30 minutes by car from the Aalto2 Museum Centre.

Alvar and Elissa Aalto designed it for themselves and built it from 1952 to 1954 as their studio and summer residence. The Aalto family used it as a summer home until 1994 (house-museum network listing).
The foundation describes it as a place where Aalto could experiment with materials, forms, techniques and proportions.
funding_verdict: Muuratsalo Experimental House: foundation-run: state subsidy, municipal grants and earnings of the Alvar Aalto Foundation's museum
wider_context: Same article: Kela said in June 2026 that its Helsinki headquarters needed extensive renovation and that funding was hard to secure; the Church of the Three Crosses in Imatra is closed, with renovation needs and lack of funding cited; the planned conversion of Paimio Sanatorium into a wellness hotel has caused debate.
The house is one of the Aalto Works sites (Alvar Aalto Foundation); the article gives no funding strain for the house itself.

press_items.title: Mari Forsberg, "Aalto Works: What responsibilities does World Heritage Listing entail?" (2026)

name: Villa Kokkonen
overview: House museum at Tuulimyllyntie 5 on the western shore of Lake Tuusula in Järvenpää, run by the city through the Järvenpää Art Museum.

Alvar Aalto designed it for the composer Joonas Kokkonen (1921 to 1996), who moved in with his family in 1969. The City of Järvenpää bought it from his estate, has owned it since 1998 and reopened it as a museum in summer 2024.
Named for Kokkonen, its first resident.
funding_verdict: Villa Kokkonen: public: City of Järvenpää, with a Ministry of Education and Culture grant

press_items.title: Mari Tossavainen, "Näyttelyarvio: Museonäyttelyssä esitellään Alvar Aallon suunnittelemaa taiteilijakotia" (2024)

name: Hvitträsk
overview: Studio home on Lake Vitträsk at Hvitträskintie 166, Luoma, Kirkkonummi, about 30 km west of Helsinki.
The architects Herman Gesellius, Armas Lindgren and Eliel Saarinen built it from 1901 to 1903 as their shared studio and home. It opened to the public in 1971.
The name means "white lake" (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Hvitträsk: state money: a site of the National Museum of Finland

name: Villa Mairea
overview: House at Pikkukoivukuja 20 in Noormarkku (Pori), with a pine forest in view from the dining room (Wikipedia).

Maire and Harry Gullichsen commissioned it. Aino and Alvar Aalto designed the building and interiors, with design work from late 1937 and construction in 1938 to 1939. It was completed in 1939. The pages read give no founding date for the Villa Mairea Foundation, which runs it.
The plan is a modified L-shape with a lawn and curved swimming pool in the angle, and the interiors use wood, stone and brick.
funding_verdict: Villa Mairea: family property owner and a foundation: no income or donor list published
wider_context: Same article: Kimmo Levä, Director General of the Finnish Heritage Agency, said upkeep still rests with the owners of World Heritage sites; Kela's Helsinki headquarters and the closed Church of the Three Crosses in Imatra are cited for lack of funding.
Villa Mairea is one of the 13 Aalto Works that Archinfo reports as listed since the end of July 2026 (the villa's own network page still says nominated), and the villa's owner is a private company.

press_items.title: Mari Forsberg, "Aalto Works: What responsibilities does World Heritage Listing entail?" (2026)

name: Fondation Hartung-Bergman
overview: Home and studios of the painters Hans Hartung (1904 to 1989) and Anna-Eva Bergman (1909 to 1987) at 182 chemin du Valbosquet, Antibes, on a two-hectare olive grove on the heights of the town.

The couple bought the land in the 1960s and built the villa and studios to their own plans. A decree of 16 February 1994 recognised the foundation as a public-utility body, and Thomas Schlesser has directed it since 2014 (French Wikipedia). The site was due to reopen on 11 May 2022 with new spaces (The Art Newspaper France, 29 April 2022).
Named for the two painters.
funding_verdict: Fondation Hartung-Bergman: self-funded: the foundation's own resources, including sales from the artists' collections

name: Fondation Vincent van Gogh Arles
overview: Art museum at 35 ter rue du Docteur-Fanton in the centre of Arles, in a UNESCO World Heritage area, showing Van Gogh paintings next to contemporary art (Foundation website).

Yolande Clergue founded the Association for the Creation of the Fondation Van Gogh in 1983. Luc Hoffmann gave the project new momentum in 2008, the foundation was established by ministerial decree on 8 July 2010, and it opened on 7 April 2014 with "Van Gogh Live!" (Foundation website; Wikipedia).
Named for Vincent van Gogh, who worked in Arles (Foundation website).
funding_verdict: Fondation Vincent van Gogh Arles: private and partner-supported, no amounts published: led by Maja Hoffmann, with the City of Arles, museums and companies as partners
wider_context: Maja Hoffmann also founded LUMA Arles at the Parc des Ateliers. The Art Newspaper (Toby Skeggs, "Arles cultural centre falls foul of planning rules", 30 June 2011) reported that the French National Commission for Historical Sites and Monuments rejected two of five building permit applications for the Gehry-designed LUMA complex because its towers would block the view of a bell tower and disturb Roman-Gallo sarcophagi. The article does not name the Fondation Van Gogh.
Hoffmann founded and heads LUMA, and is president of the Fondation Vincent van Gogh Arles (Wikipedia).

name: Luma Arles
overview: Arts centre in the Parc des Ateliers, a former railway repair yard (Architectural Record) at 35 avenue Victor Hugo, Arles. The site covers 7 hectares and includes 19th-century buildings, a Frank Gehry tower and a park by Bas Smets (LUMA Arles).
Created by the LUMA Foundation, headed by Maja Hoffmann (Wikipedia). The foundation was founded in Zurich in 2004 and LUMA Arles followed in 2013 (Wikipedia, Maja Hoffmann).
The Gehry tower opened in summer 2021 (Wikipedia, Maja Hoffmann). Hoffmann first approached Gehry in 2008 (Architectural Record, Andrew Ayers, 29 June 2021).
funding_verdict: LUMA Arles: privately funded: the LUMA Foundation of Maja Hoffmann, a Roche heiress

press_items.title: Linda Yablonsky, "What's wrong with creating an art mega-complex in Arles?" (16 August 2018)

name: Maison Louis Carré
overview: Aalto house of about 450 m² at 2 chemin du Saint-Sacrement, Bazoches-sur-Guyonne (Yvelines), on a gentle slope at the edge of the Rambouillet forest.

Alvar Aalto designed it for the Breton-born art dealer Louis Carré, whom he met at the 1956 Venice Biennale. The permit was filed in December 1956, building began in autumn 1957, and Carré and his wife Olga moved in in June 1959.
Named for Carré, its first owner. He died in 1977, Olga lived there until her death in 2002, and the art collection was sold at auction in December 2002.
funding_verdict: Maison Louis Carré: mixed: public grants, ticket sales and venue hire

name: CAPC Musée d Art Contemporain
aliases: capc musée d art contemporain bordeaux
overview: Contemporary art museum at 7 rue Ferrère in the Chartrons district of Bordeaux, served by tram line B (French Wikipedia).

Founded in 1973 as a centre for contemporary visual arts. It became the Musée d'art contemporain de la Ville de Bordeaux in 1984 and received the Musée de France label in 2002 (CAPC). French Wikipedia states that Jean-Louis Froment created it and directed it until 1996.

Building: the Entrepôt Lainé, built in 1824 as a warehouse for colonial produce and designed by the engineer Claude Deschamps. The City bought it in 1973 after it was listed on the supplementary inventory of historic monuments. Architects Denis Valode and Jean Pistre led the renovations of 1984 to 1990 and Andrée Putman was the interior designer, with nearly 3,500 square metres of exhibition space (CAPC).
funding_verdict: CAPC: municipal museum of the City of Bordeaux, with DRAC Nouvelle-Aquitaine as institutional partner and named corporate patrons
wider_context: French Wikipedia states that Karfa Diallo, director of the association Mémoires & Partages, criticised in a Mediapart op-ed of 31 August 2023 what he called "a semantic minimisation" of the Entrepôt Lainé's link to the crimes of slavery (translation). After a meeting on 21 September, the museum committed to revising its presentation text, and a memorial plaque or artwork was planned for 2024.

press_items.title: Anna Sansom, "French art world shock at sacking of Bordeaux museum director" (2018)

name: Le Consortium
overview: Contemporary art centre at 37 rue de Longvic, Dijon, about a 20-minute walk from Dijon railway station and 10 minutes on foot from the musée des Beaux-arts (Consortium Museum website).

Founded in 1977 by Xavier Douroux and Franck Gautherot, young academics who showed contemporary art on the first floor of an alternative bookstore. Éric Troncy joined in 1995 and Seungduk Kim in 2000. Later directors included Stéphanie Moisdon and Anne Pontégnie (the museum's history page).

Earlier names and moves: it grew out of the association Le Coin du Miroir. It received the Art Center label in 1982 and moved to a former appliance store. In 1983 Le Coin du Miroir, À La Limite and Déjà Vu merged. In 1991 it moved to a 4,000 m2 factory on the outskirts (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Le Consortium: mixed: French state and local government, plus private supporters

name: Appartement témoin Perret
overview: Furnished 100 m² show flat at 181 rue de Paris (house-museum network listing) in one of the Immeubles Sans Affectation Individuelle (ISAI) of the rebuilt Le Havre centre.

A reconstruction of the model flats Auguste Perret showed in Paris in 1947 and in Le Havre between 1949 and 1953. The city bought a flat in 2005, just after UNESCO listed the rebuilt centre, and the flat opened in 2006.
Named for Auguste Perret, the architect of the rebuilt centre.
funding_verdict: Appartement témoin Perret: public: City of Le Havre and Le Havre Seine Métropole
wider_context: Joseph Abram, in Lotus International 4 (1989), reported architects' criticism of Perret's Le Havre plan: Leonardo Benevolo said Perret treated the city as one architecture project and lacked a "methodology of city planning"; Manfredo Tafuri and Francesco Dal Co tied it to "technological academicism and formal academicism". Abram also quoted Pierre Dalloz calling it in 1956 "the greatest success of the French reconstruction".
Banque des Territoires (2021) wrote that residents long disliked the rebuilding before its architectural qualities gained recognition.
The flat shows Perret's housing for that reconstruction and was created by the city after the centre's UNESCO listing.

name: Van Doesburghuis
overview: Studio-house at 29 Rue Charles Infroit in Meudon-Val-Fleury, a suburb of Paris (Dutch Wikipedia, villa's site).

Theo van Doesburg and his wife Nelly commissioned it in the late 1920s. Building began in October 1929 and it was finished at the end of 1930. Van Doesburg died at 47 before it was furnished and painted (Dutch Wikipedia, villa's site).
Named for Theo van Doesburg, founder of De Stijl.
funding_verdict: Van Doesburghuis: mainly public: Dutch ministries, plus resident rent

name: Villa Majorelle
overview: Art Nouveau house at 1 rue Louis Majorelle in Nancy, run by the Musée de l'École de Nancy. The museum says it has been open to the public since 1997, and its February 2024 press kit says it reopened in February 2020 after restoration (Lorraine Mag gives 15 and 16 February).
Henri Sauvage designed it for the cabinetmaker Louis Majorelle. The museum dates it "around 1901 to 1902" and the city's patronage leaflet 1902 to 1903. The leaflet also calls it Villa Jika.
Named for Louis Majorelle (1859 to 1926).
funding_verdict: Villa Majorelle: mainly public with corporate patronage: City of Nancy, Groupe Duval (2018), Fondation TotalEnergies (October 2020)

name: Appartement-atelier Le Corbusier
overview: Duplex of 240 m² on the two top floors of the Molitor building at 24 rue Nungesser-et-Coli, Paris 16th, on the border with Boulogne-Billancourt.

Le Corbusier and Pierre Jeanneret designed the building in 1931 and completed it in early 1934 for a developer bankrupt by 1935. Le Corbusier acquired the right to occupy the top two floors, built at his own expense, and lived there from 1934 to 1965, and the Fondation Le Corbusier has owned the apartment since his death (Wikipedia, Dezeen).
The facades are glass with solid glass bricks, with a free plan, roof terrace and polychromy. The apartment was listed as a monument in 1972 and the building joined the UNESCO list in 2016.
funding_verdict: Appartement-atelier Le Corbusier: foundation-run: royalties and licence income, tickets, state support, patrons Cassina and Chanel
wider_context: Unverified: Xavier de Jarcy, in his 2015 book Le Corbusier, un fascisme français, calls Le Corbusier "an out-and-out fascist", and François Chaslin, author of Un Corbusier, says he found "anti-Semitic sketches" attributed to him (The Art Newspaper).

The Fondation calls his Vichy period an "extended stay" and its members called the controversy "manipulative" (ArchDaily); on 28 April 2015 it and the Pompidou Centre announced a research project on his wartime activities (The Art Newspaper).
None of these pieces names the apartment. The link is that the Fondation that runs it takes part of its income from licence contracts and image rights to his work (2019 and 2020 accounts).

press_items.title: Anny Shaw, "Pompidou responds to criticism that Le Corbusier exhibition glosses over architect's fascist past" (2015)
Holly Giermann, "Two New Books Claim Le Corbusier was a 'Militant Fascist'" (2015)
Natasha Levy, "Le Corbusier's Paris home reopens its doors to the public" (2018)

name: KADIST
overview: Non-profit contemporary art organisation with its hub and exhibition space at 19bis/21 rue des Trois Frères in Montmartre, Paris 18e, and staff and advisors on five continents (kadist.org).

The idea came at a family dinner in Montmartre in 2001, when the curator Sandra Terdjman proposed an art project to her uncle Vincent Worms, then a venture capitalist in San Francisco; the Paris gallery opened in 2006 (Mission Local).
Worms is president and Terdjman vice-president; both are co-founders. Joseph del Pesco is Americas director and Marie Martraire collection director (kadist.org).
funding_verdict: KADIST: private: a French family's money, through a French endowment fund and US foundations

name: Musée de la Chasse et de la Nature
aliases: musée de la chasse et de la nature paris
overview: Private museum of the relationship between people and animals, in the Marais in the 3rd arrondissement of Paris, near Rambuteau Métro station (Wikipedia).

Founded by François and Jacqueline Sommer. The Fondation François Sommer, which they created, dates from 1964 (French Wikipedia). André Malraux inaugurated the museum on 21 February 1967 (museum website).
Named for its subject, hunting and nature. The foundation carries the founder's name.
funding_verdict: Musée de la Chasse et de la Nature: privately run: the Fondation François Sommer, created by the family that owned a felt-making firm

press_items.title: Sarah Wade, chapter on Art Orienté Objet at the museum in "Revisiting the Past in Museums and at Historic Sites" (2021)
